title: Who feeds Britain? Risks, farmers' squeeze and what government must do
label: 12 October 2026 · Resilience of the UK’s food supply
summary: Witnesses from farming, retail and food manufacturing, and two academic specialists, told the Public Accounts Committee that UK food supply has been resilient so far but is increasingly fragile. Farmers face cash-flow shocks from extreme weather, high input and energy costs, and loss of subsidy protection. Retailers and manufacturers warn high taxes and energy prices discourage onshore processing and investment. Experts urged a national food strategy, clearer leadership across government, mapping of critical food infrastructure, and more local and household preparedness.

glossary.definition: Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs — the UK Government department responsible for farming, food and environment policy.
Sustainable Farming Incentive — a UK scheme paying farmers for environmentally friendly practices instead of old EU-style area payments.
A UK food-assurance label and audit scheme showing food has been produced to certain welfare, safety and traceability standards.
Facilities or services—like ports, power, water, major food sites—whose failure would threaten national life or economy.

glossary.term: basic payment scheme / single farm payment
glossary.definition: Former subsidy paid per hectare to UK farmers; its reduction or removal exposes some farmers to world market prices.

chapters.title: Big-picture risks and how the system has coped
chapters.takeaway: The UK food system has been resilient through recent shocks, but climate, energy, cyber and geopolitical risks are growing.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’re holding two sessions on food resilience. Today we want to hear if the Government can keep our food supply secure, whether farmers are prepared, and how Government works with retailers and manufacturers.

turns.speaker: Jim Bligh
turns.text: Retailers need a resilient supply chain. The system has coped—covid, Ukraine and the Iran tensions—but risks are rising: climate, energy and water, cyber-security, shifting regulation, and international trade shocks.

turns.speaker: Balwinder Dhoot
turns.text: Industry has been resilient, but domestic production is being eroded over years. Imports are growing faster than exports, and if that trend continues it will make future shocks harder to manage.

turns.speaker: Harry Metcalfe
turns.text: Farming varies across the UK. In my arable area 2026 gave the smallest harvest since records began; climate swings—flood then drought—are now common and make farming very risky.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: Government policy—rising taxes, higher energy costs, and environmental rules—are making it harder to farm and invest in production, so we need to ask if DEFRA can make the long-term plan farming needs.

chapters.title: Farmers' finances, incentives and the cash‑flow squeeze
chapters.takeaway: Farmers face high input costs, lost subsidy safety nets, and poor cash flow—so many are de-risking or reducing production.

turns.speaker: Harry Metcalfe
turns.text: Four of my five worst harvests since 2020; cash-flow is the big problem. I’ve already spent most input costs before harvest. The removal of area payments exposed many English farmers to world prices.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You mentioned the SFI. Did the scheme give farmers stability?

turns.speaker: Harry Metcalfe
turns.text: SFI pays for environmental actions and I support that, but it doesn’t encourage me to grow more food now. The timing and short windows to apply clash with farming seasons.

turns.speaker: Jim Bligh
turns.text: Retailers can build long-term partnerships to help finance farm investment, but profit matters—profit enables investment and resilience. Industry also needs clear, long-term government direction to back that investment.

turns.speaker: Balwinder Dhoot
turns.text: Resilience equals investment. If businesses can’t make money here they move processing overseas and stop buying British ingredients. We need a market that encourages onshore investment, not forces it out.

turns.speaker: Mr Betts
turns.text: Should supermarkets be clearer about where products come from so consumers can choose to support British farmers?

turns.speaker: Harry Metcalfe
turns.text: Yes. Packaging rules currently mean origin can be obscured by where something is packed. Traceability systems like Red Tractor exist and should be used to show genuine British provenance.

chapters.title: Processing, energy and the shifting supply chain
chapters.takeaway: High energy and other costs push processing offshore; losing domestic processing capacity weakens resilience if imports fall during shocks.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is the decline in UK processing a threat — coffee roasted abroad, fewer abattoirs — and does that matter for resilience?

turns.speaker: Jim Bligh
turns.text: Yes. Processing is energy‑intensive and UK energy costs are high, which discourages investment. If processing moves, the ingredients and jobs move too, and we lose onshore capacity.

turns.speaker: Balwinder Dhoot
turns.text: Energy often represents at least 10% of input costs for manufacturers. If the UK is twice as expensive as competitors, investors will locate elsewhere and buy ingredients locally there, not in Britain.

turns.speaker: Harry Metcalfe
turns.text: On the farm side, grain markets are global: farmers can sell forward, but bad harvests expose growers when contracted volumes are higher than what they produce. That risk discourages planting.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: Taxes like the upcoming carbon border measures and higher energy costs are stacking up against farmers and processors. That policy mix risks hollowing out onshore food production.

chapters.title: Government capability, DEFRA and the need for a food strategy
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses say DEFRA lacks sustained leadership and cross-government authority; experts call for a clear national food policy and stronger coordination.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: Is DEFRA fit for purpose on long-term planning and administering schemes? Farmers say the SFI window was badly managed and payments late.

turns.speaker: Jim Bligh
turns.text: DEFRA is an economic department but doesn’t always act like one across Government. There isn’t a clear long-term steer, and officials struggle to arbitrate policy trade-offs that affect food costs.

turns.speaker: Professor Tim Lang
turns.text: We need a proper national food policy, not just a farming or environment policy. Policy has been fragmented for years; without clear purpose—what food is for—planning and investment won’t follow.

turns.speaker: Professor Neil Ward
turns.text: DEFRA is small and historically set up for rural affairs, not a full systems role. Resilience needs cross‑government co-ordination; we recommended a national governance body to convene industry, health and communities.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The NAO warned DEFRA is less confident about business ability to cope without government intervention in five to 10 years. That underlines the need for better strategy and leadership.

chapters.title: Critical infrastructure, local planning and community resilience
chapters.takeaway: Map and protect critical food nodes, involve local partnerships, and strengthen household and community preparedness rather than leaving it all to markets.

turns.speaker: Mr Betts
turns.text: Should parts of the food chain be on the critical national infrastructure (CNI) database?

turns.speaker: Jim Bligh
turns.text: Yes. We should identify critical assets—ports, large depots, major processing centres—and ensure plans exist to give them priority in crises, for fuel, power and workforce access.

turns.speaker: Balwinder Dhoot
turns.text: You don’t need to capture every small actor, but you must identify critical nodes whose failure would cut food availability and test their resilience to fuel, power or staffing shortages.

turns.speaker: Professor Tim Lang
turns.text: Include local institutions too: food partnerships, community stores and sub-national authorities. Countries like Sweden and the Netherlands treat multi-level planning seriously—England needs that approach.

turns.speaker: Rachel Gilmour
turns.text: How do we ensure vulnerable people get food in a severe disruption — and how much should households be expected to prepare?

turns.speaker: Professor Neil Ward
turns.text: We need three things together: strengthen production resilience, map and protect supply nodes, and make healthy food affordable and accessible. Community groups fill gaps, but Government must back that with funding and planning.

turns.speaker: Professor Tim Lang
turns.text: Households can help with short-term preparedness, but resilience relies on neighbourhood and city-level plans and modest local storage. Reliance solely on individual prepping would be unfair and ineffective.

chapters.title: International lessons and concrete asks
chapters.takeaway: Look to countries that plan multi-level food security, buy-in long-term investment, map critical nodes and create a national food plan backed by clear leadership.

turns.speaker: Matt Turmaine
turns.text: Which countries do this well and what can we copy?

turns.speaker: Professor Neil Ward
turns.text: Finland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Israel and Singapore all take food resilience seriously. Study their institutional set-ups: national plans plus strong regional capabilities.

turns.speaker: Professor Tim Lang
turns.text: We should give sub-national authorities more powers for food plans, build networked supply chains (not single choke points), and unlock investment by setting a stable, long-term policy framework.

turns.speaker: Jim Bligh
turns.text: Industry can form long-term contracts with farmers to underpin investment, but Government must reduce policy volatility and consider targeted support for energy or other industrial costs for food processing.

turns.speaker: Balwinder Dhoot
turns.text: The essence is investment: encourage onshore processing, de-risk energy and cyber risks, and create incentives to keep factories and supply chains in the UK where that supports resilience.

turns.speaker: Harry Metcalfe
turns.text: My single ask: understand farming as a long-term, seasonal business. Don’t expect farmers to operate like short-term commercial firms; give policies and payments that work with farming timeframes so we keep growing food.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you to all witnesses. We’ll follow up with officials on Thursday and probe how Government intends to act on mapping critical assets, leadership for a food plan, and the support farmers need.
